food-1-043.title: Distinguishing raw-material hazards and microbial controls
food-1-043.objective: Explain hazard types and control targets using the textbook’s concrete examples.

paragraphs.p1: Hard plastic fragments and eggshell left behind can cause harm through hardness or sharp edges. Poor storage of tuna, horse mackerel, sardines or mackerel can allow histamine to increase and cause allergy-like symptoms. A fish’s name or appearance alone does not establish safety.
paragraphs.p2: Campylobacter, Salmonella and enterohemorrhagic E. coli multiply in the body. Vibrio parahaemolyticus multiplies and produces toxins there; some enterohemorrhagic E. coli also produce toxins. The textbook says bacterial growth slows at 10°C or below, is almost absent at 4°C or below, and stops at −15°C or below. These figures do not mean sterilization. Bacteria can grow again from endospores, and mold spores are widespread, so storage control and cleaning must continue.
paragraphs.p3: Bivalves such as oysters may carry norovirus. It multiplies in the human intestine, not in food. The textbook says alcohol disinfection alone does not kill it and describes washing equipment, then immersing it in 200 ppm sodium hypochlorite solution or wiping it with a cloth wetted with that solution. Distinguish this from chemical treatment of food; actual work follows the workplace’s approved procedures.

food-1-043.activity: Make a three-column table of target and purpose for fish storage, low-temperature bacterial control and norovirus equipment treatment. Explain why textbook examples cannot become operating conditions for every product.
food-1-043.summary: Distinguish hazard type, growth location and treatment target. Do not confuse cold storage with sterilization.

food-1-044.title: Checking every detail of workwear before entry
food-1-044.objective: Explain the clothing, hair and mask checks in the illustrations against your workplace’s rules.

paragraphTitles.p2: Checks shown in the workwear illustration

paragraphs.p1: The textbook’s general order is to arrange the hair, put on a hairnet, cap and workwear, then check in a mirror. Hairpins, false eyelashes and accessories can also become foreign material. Keep nails short and return unnecessary belongings to their designated place before entering.
paragraphs.p2: The illustration gives examples of a standing collar, a button-free undershirt, clean outer workwear without pockets or buttons, and gathered cuffs and hems. Tuck the ends of the outer and inner shirts into the trousers, and wear required aprons and arm covers over the workwear. Check the complete outfit specified by your workplace rather than copying one part of the picture.
paragraphs.p3: Tie up the hair and contain it in the net and cap. Understand why the illustration shows a cap worn deeply with its lower part tucked into the outer garment. Cover the nose to chin with the mask, shape the nose wire and leave no gaps beside the nose or cheeks. Use properly sized gloves without tears or dirt. Remove remaining hair and dust with a sticky roller or the specified equipment.

food-1-044.activity: Use the illustration to explain six checks: hair, collar, cuffs, hems, mask and gloves. If your workplace’s clothing differs, identify whom to ask instead of changing it on your own.
food-1-044.summary: Entry checks include coverage, gaps, tucked clothing and carried items, not only cleanliness.

food-1-045.title: Distinguishing management systems from inspection
food-1-045.objective: Explain the different purposes of HACCP, workplace prevention measures and microbiological testing.

paragraphTitles.p1: HACCP and the foundation of hygiene management

paragraphs.p1: HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point: analyzing hazards and controlling critical points. It does not remove the foundation of general hygiene management. Examine each food’s hazards and process, then combine the controls required.
paragraphs.p2: The textbook gives examples of pocket-free workwear to prevent unnecessary items being brought in, and entry records or cameras to check work. It does not say every factory needs identical equipment. The example of producing allergen-containing products at the end of the day and cleaning afterward is also a workplace production-plan example.
paragraphs.p3: The textbook distinguishes legally required testing from voluntary testing. Typical voluntary items include the standard plate count, E. coli and coliforms; Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella or Campylobacter may also be tested. It mentions equipment temperatures of −15°C or below for freezers and 10°C or below for refrigerators. Read these separately from raw-material storage conditions. Current legal requirements need separate verification; actual work must check the food concerned and workplace rules.

food-1-045.activity: Sort today’s examples into systems that prevent hazards, systems that check implementation and systems that test products, then explain the differences.
food-1-045.summary: Do not confuse basic hygiene, workplace-specific measures, test items, or equipment and raw-material temperatures.

food-1-046.title: Choose protective equipment and use finger pointing and calling
food-1-046.objective: Explain equipment materials and purposes, then check with your finger and voice before work.

paragraphTitles.p1: Protect the head, eyes, ears and feet
paragraphTitles.p3: Check with your finger, voice and partner

paragraphs.p1: The supplied textbook describes using a helmet to protect the head when working at a height of 2 m or more. This is the textbook explanation; check workplace instructions for actual work. Use goggles for eyes, earplugs for noise, and reinforced safety shoes against crushing injuries to feet. Equipment for a different purpose is not a substitute.
paragraphs.p2: Mexcel gloves are cut-resistant knitted-fibre gloves; chain gloves are cut-resistant stainless-steel mesh gloves. Choose the specified heat-resistant mittens for hot objects and the specified heat-resistant apron for heat, chemicals and cleaning. Even with rubber gloves, putting a hand into hot liquid can let liquid enter through the opening.
paragraphs.p3: Finger pointing and calling means pointing to the object and saying its name or state to confirm it. Fictional example: complete the prescribed check while saying “Before starting: surroundings checked.” Do not start if signals are not understood. Warn someone acting dangerously and inform the responsible person before leaving your station.
paragraphs.p4: Goggles protect eyes from chemicals, fine powder and splashes during high-pressure cleaning. Steel or plastic reinforcement at the toes and heels of safety shoes protects against crushing injuries. Covered boots have oil-resistant, slip-resistant soles, and an upper cover helps keep hot water and other liquids out. Check the body area and mechanism protected, not just the equipment name.

food-1-046.activity: Compare the purposes of five protective items, then practise finger pointing and calling and confirming signals. About 30 minutes total.
food-1-046.summary: Choose protection by purpose and combine pointing, calling and confirmation with the other person.

food-1-047.title: Learn prevention from accident data
food-1-047.objective: Distinguish historical accident data from a schematic ratio and anticipate small hazards.

paragraphTitles.p1: Read the figures as historical data
paragraphTitles.p2: Do not turn a ratio into a prediction
paragraphTitles.p3: Connect objects to harm to people

paragraphs.p1: The Reiwa 4 (2022) data printed in edition 5.1 show falls on the same level at 31.3%, caught-in or entanglement accidents at 19.2%, cuts or abrasions at 10.8%, falls from height at 8.4%, and other accidents at 31.3%. The top three account for about 60%. The textbook defines inexperienced workers as those with under 3 years of experience and says they account for about half of food-manufacturing accidents. These are figures from that source period, not current statistics. These printed values total 101.0%. The original statistics have not been cross-checked, so do not treat this breakdown as validated.
paragraphs.p2: The textbook’s Heinrich relationship links 1 serious accident, 29 minor injuries or similar events, and 300 near misses. It is not a formula predicting the same ratio in every factory. Its learning purpose is to record small warning signs and discuss causes and controls together.
paragraphs.p3: Risk prediction training (KYT) links events such as leaks, fire, explosions and falling objects to poisoning, oxygen deficiency, burns and fractures. Fictional example: if you suspect a gas flame has gone out, stay away from the hazard, tell nearby people and the responsible person, and follow emergency procedures. Do not expose yourself to danger to test it.
paragraphs.p4: A same-level fall can cause head or back impact and fractures; a fall from height can cause sprains and fractures. Entanglement can crush fingers or arms and may be fatal. Blades can cause cuts or finger amputation; heat can burn the face or whole body. Back pain from heavy loads can persist or recur. Heat illness and collisions with fast-moving vehicles can also be life-threatening.

food-1-047.activity: Identify the top three types in the historical accident data and explain the limits of the ratio. Share one fictional near miss. About 30 minutes total.
food-1-047.summary: Use historical figures to support prevention, not as a guarantee of present safety.

food-1-048.title: Check lifting movements and work in heat
food-1-048.objective: Turn detailed lifting, heat and daily-control checks into concrete actions.

paragraphTitles.p1: Keep the load close to the body
paragraphTitles.p2: Prepare for heat and respond early

paragraphs.p1: Before lifting, consider weight, footing, a helper and a trolley. If lifting is appropriate, move close to the load, bend your knees and lower your hips, hold the load, then rise slowly while extending your knees. Do not force a lift while twisting. This sequence alone does not make every load safe.
paragraphs.p2: In heat, combine breathable, absorbent, quick-drying clothing with food-hygiene dress requirements. If symptoms occur, follow workplace procedures for reporting, moving to a cool place, resting, loosening clothing and cooling the neck, armpits and groin. The source also gives salt-containing water and sports drinks as examples. Decide whether drinking is appropriate from the person’s condition and emergency procedures; never force fluids.
paragraphs.p3: Standardizing in 5S concerns infection prevention for workers as well as food. Define common routes and places for tools and materials. Fasten long-sleeved cuffs and do not roll sleeves up. Perform planned maintenance even during busy production. Record facts at measurement time; do not batch records later or amend them on your own.

food-1-048.activity: Draw the lifting sequence and explain the first response in heat and a daily checklist. About 30 minutes total.
food-1-048.summary: Manage posture, physical condition and daily checks, avoiding strain and unauthorized decisions.

food-2-037.title: Turn workplace and daily-life rules into action
food-2-037.objective: Confirm roles and reporting routes, and choose specific actions for daily life, commuting and hygiene.

paragraphTitles.p1: Check roles and use brief teaching opportunities

paragraphs.p1: An organization may let the supervisor communicate directly with workers or through a team leader. Do not infer authority from a title alone; check your own workplace’s instruction and reporting routes. OJT can take place when assignments change, during safe waiting periods, when receiving reports or questions, in meetings and while working together. Each time, combine one goal, a brief demonstration, the learner’s own performance and a check.
paragraphs.p2: Tell the other person if you will be late; check local instructions for waste categories, collection places and days. Avoid loud nighttime noise, littering and spitting in public. When cycling, keep to the left of the roadway and give pedestrians priority even where signs permit pavement cycling. Use a light at night. Do not cycle after drinking alcohol or while operating a smartphone; protect your head with a helmet. On trains and buses, queue, keep doorways clear and offer priority seats to people who need them. Check current official guidance for specific traffic regulations.
paragraphs.p3: At meals, do not stab food with chopsticks or pull dishes toward you with them; hold rice and soup bowls in your hand. Wash before entering a shared bath and do not splash others. Use the designated toilet paper, flush no other paper and clean any mess you make. Dry washed hands hygienically; do not flick water away or wipe them on clothing. Wear a mask when coughing; for a sudden cough, cover your mouth with a handkerchief or elbow. Build habits of keeping food bags and work clothing off dirty floors and not leaving waste or used utensils unattended. Supervisors should practise these habits themselves and support coworkers’ 5S.

food-2-037.activity: Read for 10 minutes: write down reporting routes and where to check daily-life guidance. Practise for 15 minutes: choose one commuting situation, one shared-living situation and one brief OJT opportunity; explain the action and reason. Check for 5 minutes: choose a hygiene habit to continue from tomorrow.
food-2-037.summary: Check roles in the actual organization and turn consideration for others and hygiene habits into specific actions.

food-2-038.title: Check the scope of concerns and statistical denominators
food-2-038.objective: Refer diverse concerns to the organization and explain figures after checking the population, year and denominator.

paragraphTitles.p1: Do not restrict concerns to a narrow category
paragraphTitles.p2: The same percentage can concern different populations
paragraphTitles.p3: Handle statistics and consultation records differently

paragraphs.p1: Besides abuse of authority, sexual conduct and harassment concerning pregnancy, childbirth, childcare or family care, watch for disability-related insults, abusive customer conduct and conduct during recruitment. These can affect health, ability and continued employment. Supervisors should not make legal determinations alone: organize the facts and refer the matter to a manager or designated contact under the consultation procedure. The company promotes awareness and training, and people in management should also review their own words and actions.
paragraphs.p2: This is a fictional exercise. If qualifying cases are confirmed at 10 of 40 companies that received concerns, the proportion is 25％. It concerns companies that received concerns, not all companies or all workers. In another fictional example, cause A involves 3 incidents and 6 patients, while B involves 1 incident and 20 patients. The leading cause differs depending on whether incidents or patients are counted. Compare figures using consistent populations, counting methods, periods and denominators.
paragraphs.p3: For published surveys, check the survey year, who or which companies were questioned, and the sample size for each item. Do not present past figures as the current rate. Consultation records are not for disclosure to the entire workplace for statistical purposes. Separate when, where and what happened from speculation, and share only what is needed to respond. Check current official information and the company’s responsible contact about the application of specific rules.

food-2-038.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize types of concerns and reporting contacts. Analyse for 15 minutes: explain the 40 companies, 10 companies and 25％ in the fictional example; compare 3 incidents/6 patients with 1 incident/20 patients using both measures. Check for 5 minutes: distinguish facts that need sharing from personal information that must not be spread.
food-2-038.summary: Take concerns seriously, refer them through the organization, and read statistics with explicit populations, years and denominators.

food-2-039.title: Connect product conditions to approved cleaning procedures
food-2-039.objective: Consider controls based on product characteristics and soil, and verify the approved procedure version and product disposition.

paragraphTitles.p1: Do not decide with product conditions left blank
paragraphTitles.p2: Compare powder, meat, vegetables and oil
paragraphTitles.p3: Check the procedure and its version together

paragraphs.p1: Product descriptions should identify ingredients, heat treatment or its absence, intended consumers, packaging, solid or liquid form, moisture content, pH, and transport and storage conditions. Filling in water activity, a different measure, does not fill in the moisture-content field. Record unknown conditions and whom to ask. If allergen or metal-fragment contamination is suspected, prevent shipment and isolate and handle the product under the defined procedure and authority. Do not assume reheating, dilution or picking out visible fragments makes it safe.
paragraphs.p2: In powder processes, check ventilation equipment and gaps for deposits and confirm equipment-appropriate methods such as vacuum or brush collection. Where meat fragments or fat remain, follow the approved SSOP for residue removal, washing, rinsing and drying. Confirm neutral or mildly alkaline detergent use and warm-water conditions for each target; do not transfer another factory’s example unchanged. Do not apply a vegetable-fragment flushing method unchanged to a grease trap: collect the oil. Also check that soil is not spread to surrounding areas.
paragraphs.p3: Specify the SSOP’s target, chemicals, utensils, frequency, method, operator, acceptance criteria, inspection, abnormality response and records. Check the creation date, revision date, version, preparer and approver on its cover. If old and new copies are mixed, do not choose independently: confirm the effective approved version and withdraw old copies. Explain changes to workers and verify they can perform them. Improve through verification and records, protecting the cleanliness of both the target equipment and its surroundings.

food-2-039.activity: Read for 10 minutes: make a product-condition card and an SSOP checklist. Compare for 15 minutes: separate the conditions to check for airborne powder and remaining oil; write the communication and withdrawal flow when two versions are found. Check for 5 minutes: explain why suspect product must not be shipped on personal judgement.
food-2-039.summary: Check product conditions and soil, use the current approved procedure, and leave no ambiguity about suspect food disposition.

food-2-040.title: Choose cleaning and disinfection for the soil and material
food-2-040.objective: Distinguish detergent properties, temperature and disinfection methods, and explain conditions to check in an approved procedure.

paragraphs.p1: The textbook gives approximate ranges: neutral around pH6–8, alkaline pH8 or above, acidic pH6 or below. The boundaries overlap. Oils/proteins and mineral scale require different suitable detergents; pH11 or above is also given as a strong-alkali hazard example. Follow manufacturer instructions and approved procedures in actual work.
paragraphs.p2: Collecting residue first reduces cleaning and wastewater loads. The textbook explains protein coagulation at 60℃ or above, so hotter water is not always better. Check washing, rinsing, draining/drying and reassembly conditions in the equipment procedure. Draining and drying are not the same.
paragraphs.p3: Select immersion, heat, ultraviolet or spraying according to the part's material, shape, chemical resistance and heat resistance. Check gloves and goggles for spraying and what disinfection/rinsing the CIP program includes. Do not independently change concentration or duration, or guarantee disinfection from ATP alone.

food-2-040.activity: For a greasy part, list what to check about soil, material, temperature, protective equipment and manufacturer instructions.
food-2-040.summary: Cleaning and disinfection have different purposes. Check soil, material and temperature, and keep to approved conditions.

food-2-041.title: Connect inspection, equipment and label checks
food-2-041.objective: Distinguish inspection purposes and explain information to check in the equipment register and product label.

paragraphTitles.p2: Match the register to the actual instrument
paragraphTitles.p3: Check label information against materials and packaging

paragraphs.p1: Microbiological inspection includes surface swabbing and settle-plate testing of microorganisms falling from the air. ATP is a rapid indicator of organic soil, not proof of disinfection. Distinguish what each result examined so the manager can evaluate it.
paragraphs.p2: Record instrument ID, use, required accuracy, calibration method/person/date, next due date and whether use is permitted. Match the actual ID to the calibration record. Ask the responsible department about legally required inspections and external bodies; do not confuse these with voluntary in-process calibration.
paragraphs.p3: The textbook lists quantity, ingredients/origin, dates/storage/use instructions, allergens and nutrition. Check the official label specification for each product against the actual materials and packaging. Stop using mismatched items and report to the responsible person; do not decide applicability yourself.
paragraphs.p4: The attached textbook describes “hygiene management based on HACCP,” following all 12 steps, and “hygiene management incorporating the HACCP approach,” using sector guides to manage under the 7 principles. It states steps 1–5 are not mandatory in the latter, but supervisors in either type of workplace learn all 12 steps. Confirm actual regulatory applicability through the responsible department’s official information.
paragraphs.p5: In the original learning diagram: 1 receipt, 2 storage, 3 mixing, 4 packing, 5 dispatch, 6 disposal/recovery, 7 washing, 8 wastewater. A/B are raw materials, P packaging and W wash water. A/B follow 1→2→3, P 2→4, food 3→4→5. Check empty containers flowing to 6 and W through 7→8. Food-only arrows can omit hazard pathways.

food-2-041.activity: Given a mismatched instrument ID and calibration record plus packaging left from the previous product, explain checks needed before use.
food-2-041.summary: Check separately, then connect inspection purpose, instrument identification/calibration and agreement between labels and actual contents.

food-2-042.title: Check normal-distribution calculations and centre changes
food-2-042.objective: Read normal-distribution percentages and 3σ ranges, then check a fictional centre-change proposal against the specification.

paragraphs.p1: Assuming a stable normal distribution, mean ±1σ contains approximately 68.3%, ±2σ 95.4%, and ±3σ 99.7%. This model is symmetric about the mean. These figures do not apply unconditionally to every dataset; product specifications and process control limits are also different concepts.
paragraphs.p2: For learning, take a specification of 46–54g, mean 50g and σ0.8g. 3σ is 2.4g, the range is 47.6–52.4g and the margin to the lower specification is 1.6g. A proposed mean of 49.5g gives 47.1–51.9g. This fictional calculation does not guarantee conformity of every product.
paragraphs.p3: Moving the mean differs from improving equipment precision to reduce σ. If variation remains large, changing only the centre can increase out-of-specification products on the other side. Actual changes require checking quality, labelling conditions and process stability, then approval by the authorised department.
paragraphs.p4: Fictional defect counts for causes A–E are A12, B7, C19, D4, E8. The horizontal axis is cause category and the vertical axis is count. C is highest at 19, D lowest at 4, a difference of 15. Read values from bar lengths and explain why counts alone do not determine safety severity or action priority.

food-2-042.activity: Calculate mean ±3σ in the fictional example; explain the lower margin before/after the change and conditions to check before approval.
food-2-042.summary: Distinguish distribution assumptions, centre, variation and specifications. Calculations alone do not authorise a change or guarantee every product.

food-2-043.title: Align the conditions behind charts and indicators
food-2-043.objective: Check distributions, records, control lines and monetary definitions, then test proposed causes.

paragraphTitles.p2: Read each kind of chart appropriately

paragraphs.p1: The six histogram shapes—ordinary, two-peaked, comb-like, long-tailed, cliff-like and isolated-island—do not establish causes. Check mixed populations, bin design and selection history. Define measurement precision and boundary assignment. The source suggests the square root of the sample count as a starting point for bin count, not a fixed rule. Two peaks or an isolated island suggest mixed groups; comb-like gaps suggest checking bins, a long tail one-sided control, and a cliff selection effects. An ordinary shape alone does not prove stability. In the comparison figure: A ordinary, B comb-like, C long-tailed, D cliff-like, E two-peaked, F isolated-island.
paragraphs.p2: Scatterplots can show positive, negative, absent or nonlinear association. Pair two measurements from the same subject; association alone does not prove causation. Compare proportions with stacked bars or circles, and multiple characteristics with a radar chart using common scales. Align axes and aggregation conditions. Positive association rises rightward, negative falls; no association has little regularity, while nonlinear association is curved. In the comparison figure: A positive association, B negative association, C curved relationship, D no clear relationship.
paragraphs.p3: In a fictional record, day one has 3 packaging defects and 2 dirt defects; day two has 1 and 4. Each day totals 5, the category totals are 4 and 6, and the overall total is 10. In a fishbone diagram, place the result at the arrowhead and organize possible material, equipment and method factors on branches. Check actual objects and records.
paragraphs.p4: Source examples include a point beyond a limit, 9 points on one side, 6 rising or falling points, 14 alternating points, 2 of 3 or 4 of 5 near a limit, 15 near the center, and 8 away from the center. These are separate from product specifications. Check the decision conditions and responses adopted at your workplace. Side bias suggests a shifted center, continuous trends a moving mean, regularity outside influences, central clustering small variation, and avoidance of the center mixed populations. These are investigative hypotheses.
paragraphs.p5: Assume a fictional 10-hour run makes 200 kg, with sales of 180,000 yen and material, labor and energy costs of 70,000, 30,000 and 10,000 yen. Define value added here as the 70,000-yen difference: 7,000 yen/hour. If 2 people each work 10 hours, that is 20 person-hours and 3,500 yen/person-hour. This is neither sales nor accounting profit; check company cost categories. Here physical output is 20 kg/hour or 10 kg/person-hour; sales are 18,000 yen/hour or 9,000 yen/person-hour. These are different indicators.
paragraphs.p6: Company environmental measures include energy and labor savings, renewable energy, and changes to production or ordering processes. Compare totals and indicators per product when assessing investment. Reserving capacity downstream is also a proposal dependent on variability and equipment conditions, not a rule forcing the same capacity order on every line.

food-2-043.activity: Read for 10 minutes: organize chart purposes and indicator denominators. Work for 15 minutes: draw a record sheet and cause diagram, then calculate monetary indicators. Check for 5 minutes: explain why reference control-chart patterns must not be confused with workplace rules.
food-2-043.summary: Use comparable conditions and distinguish hypotheses, specifications and accounting definitions.

food-2-044.title: Yield denominators and hidden losses
food-2-044.objective: Derive good output from reject quantities and compare ratios using sales units and different ingredient bases.

paragraphTitles.p1: When good output cannot be weighed directly
paragraphTitles.p2: Investigate even with no rejected products
paragraphTitles.p3: Changing the denominator reverses the evaluation

paragraphs.p1: All conditions below are fictional teaching examples. If process A receives 120 kg and has no loss other than 12 kg of rejects, good output sent to B is 108 kg. A yields 108÷120=90%. Even without direct weighing, subtract rejects from input when the material-balance assumptions are established.
paragraphs.p2: Assume B makes 90 bags specified at 1 kg, with actual total mass 99 kg. Output credited on a bag-count basis is 90 kg: B yields about 83.3% from 90÷108, and overall yield is 90÷120=75%. Investigate B's 9 kg physical mass reduction separately from 9 kg filled above specification. Any reduction must preserve quality, labeling and required quantity.
paragraphs.p3: In another fictional example, 4 kg rice plus 6 kg water gives 9 kg; after a change, 4 kg rice plus 5 kg water gives 8.4 kg. On total input, yield rises from 90% to about 93.3%; on rice alone, it falls from 225% to 210%. Check comparable quality and treatment of water costs. Do not choose a recipe from the percentages alone.
paragraphs.p4: Removing bones or damaged parts and losing moisture during specified heating can be necessary for quality. When buying preprocessed ingredients, define control targets according to the processing actually done in your factory. Compare where losses arise, including labor and energy already used in later processes.
paragraphs.p5: Productivity rises when more output uses the same input, or the same output uses less input. It also rises when output grows proportionally more than increasing input, or input falls proportionally more than decreasing output. Keep units and quality conditions comparable.

food-2-044.activity: Read for 10 minutes: identify each numerator and denominator. Calculate for 15 minutes: recompute A, B and overall yields and the two rice bases; round only displayed results to one decimal place. Check for 5 minutes: explain why B deserves priority investigation and which quality conditions must be retained.
food-2-044.summary: Define good output and sales units, and separate necessary processing from avoidable loss.

food-2-045.title: Manage clock-time records and equipment precision
food-2-045.objective: Calculate time excluding planned stops and weighted averages, then use precision and maintenance records for improvement.

paragraphTitles.p3: Record subgroup means and ranges together
paragraphTitles.p4: Boundaries between trial running and maintenance

paragraphs.p1: A fictional plan runs 8:30–12:00 and 13:00–16:00, totaling 390 minutes. Actual work starts at 8:50 and stops from 10:10 to 10:25. Exclude the planned lunch stop, then subtract the 20-minute delay and 15-minute stop: actual running time is 355 minutes. Availability is 355÷390, about 91.0%. Record stop reasons by time period. A progress chart uses time and cumulative output axes, comparing the standard line with workplace-defined upper and lower tolerance bands.
paragraphs.p2: In this example, morning running time is 175 minutes at 8 kg/min and afternoon time is 180 minutes at 10 kg/min, with no rejects and a standard of 10 kg/min. Output is 3,200 kg; mean speed is 3200÷355, about 9.014 kg/min. Against planned output of 3,900 kg, the ratio is about 82.1%. Verify with original values rather than multiplying rounded availability and speed ratios.
paragraphs.p3: For fictional groups of 3 measurements, 10, 11 and 12 g have mean 11 g and range 2 g; 9, 11 and 13 g have the same mean but range 4 g. Separate charts tracking subgroup means and ranges can help. Set measurement frequency according to equipment and workplace rules. The source's 30–60-minute example is not an obligation for all equipment. The paired mean-and-range method is called an x̄-R control chart.
paragraphs.p4: At startup, check cleaning residue and lubricating oil; after prescribed safety checks, use an authorized trial run to check unusual sound and vibration. At shutdown, record damage, replacement and adjustment details too. Do not independently release isolation during cleaning or maintenance. Request specialist repairs from the responsible staff.
paragraphs.p5: Assume 200 kg of output uses 1 m³ of water, then 300 kg uses 1.2 m³. Total water rises, but consumption per product falls from 0.005 to 0.004 m³/kg. Check both wastewater quantity and contamination, and collect residue first. Do not improve indicators by removing necessary cleaning or safety stops.

food-2-045.activity: Read for 10 minutes: tabulate planned and actual clock times. Calculate for 15 minutes: derive 355 minutes, 3,200 kg and 82.1%, then plot subgroup means and ranges. Check for 5 minutes: explain why measurement frequency and authority for trial runs must be confirmed at the workplace.
food-2-045.summary: Retain time, denominator and precision conditions, and judge improvements while protecting safety and quality.

food-2-046.title: Safety details and preparations for emergencies and return to work
food-2-046.objective: Make reporting, workplace improvement, emergency and return-to-work checks concrete.

paragraphTitles.p4: Observe changes and support return to work

paragraphs.p1: The textbook gives an example of collecting near-miss reports on a designated form at the end of work. Check the actual reporting method and share hazard information promptly. Inattention calls for communication and attention cues; shortcuts and omissions also require reviewing organisational habits and systems that support following rules.
paragraphs.p2: Check temperature, humidity, noise and vibration, then compare conditions after equipment or layout improvements. Discuss rounded sharp corners, barriers preventing hand entry and remote operation with the responsible staff. A lighter heavy door may reduce injury severity. Combine protection, clothing and working-time adjustments for remaining burdens.
paragraphs.p3: Confirm the location and inspection of first-aid supplies, designated responders and training. Where oxygen deficiency or gas hazards exist, also confirm suitable protective-equipment maintenance and inspection with responsible staff. Do not attempt unprotected rescue; obtain specialist response. Even if a destination was researched beforehand, follow the ambulance team’s directions during actual transport.
paragraphs.p4: Observe changes in lateness, early departure, absence, excessive overtime or holiday work, efficiency or judgement, results, conversation, expression or movement, unusual speech or dress and cleanliness, mistakes or accidents, and toilet frequency. These observations do not establish a diagnosis. For someone returning after leave, coordinate work and environment with supervisors and occupational physicians under company policy. Share personal information only as needed.

food-2-046.activity: Read 10 minutes: organise the four checking situations. Practise 15 minutes: propose improvements for a hypothetical workplace with noise and inadequate inspections. Check 5 minutes: explain whom to consult and what to confirm for emergencies and return-to-work support.
food-2-046.summary: Make reporting, environment, emergency and return-to-work arrangements concrete and coordinate safely with specialists.

food-2-047.title: Practising severity and risk-table reading
food-2-047.objective: Separate likelihood and severity, then choose action using a hypothetical assessment rule.

paragraphs.p1: Consider likelihood from protective-cover conditions and possible contact with hazards. Distinguish death or permanent impairment, injuries causing time off work, injuries without time off, and minor injuries allowing return after treatment. Low likelihood does not justify ignoring severe consequences.
paragraphs.p2: This exercise alone multiplies likelihood 1–4 by severity 1–4. A score of 12 or more is high: act immediately and stop work until measures are completed. Scores 4–9 are medium: act promptly; stopping until completion is desirable. Scores 1–3 are low: take measures as needed. These are not actual workplace criteria.
paragraphs.p3: In the example, likelihood 2 and severity 4 give 2×4＝8, which is medium. Do not stop at the score: check the prescribed measures and stopping conditions. In practice, confirm the company table and responsible decision maker; do not mix figures or criteria from different tables.

food-2-047.activity: Read 10 minutes: compare four severity categories. Calculate for 15 minutes: use the hypothetical rule to classify 1×2, 2×3 and 3×4 and state the actions. Check 5 minutes: explain why these figures cannot be used arbitrarily at work.
food-2-047.summary: Check likelihood, severity, assessment and required action separately.

food-2-048.title: Organising textbook systems and standards by purpose
food-2-048.objective: Distinguish the purposes of references in the April 2026 edition; ask responsible departments about current applicability.

paragraphTitles.p1: Connect prevention systems and company response
paragraphTitles.p4: Check safety roles and updated information

paragraphs.p1: The textbook relates power harassment to the Comprehensive Labour Policy Promotion Act, sexual and pregnancy/childbirth harassment to the Equal Employment Opportunity Act, and childcare/family-care leave harassment to the Childcare and Family Care Leave Act. Supervisors use company consultation procedures rather than deciding legal questions alone.
paragraphs.p2: In the textbook, ISO9001 concerns quality, ISO14001 the environment and ISO22000 food-safety management. FSSC22000 also features prerequisite programmes; SQF covers the food chain from primary production through processing, transport and distribution; JFS-C is a system developed in Japan. Certification and recognition conditions can change by edition. Confirm the company’s scope and requirements.
paragraphs.p3: For cattle and beef, learn transmission of individual identification numbers; for rice, transaction records and origin information. Distinguish the purposes of the Food Recycling Act—preventing food waste and promoting recycling; the Food Loss Reduction Promotion Act—reducing food loss; and the plastics legislation—reducing discharge, collecting and recycling resources.
paragraphs.p4: The textbook’s safety manager and hygiene manager respectively manage technical safety and hygiene matters. OSHMS and ISO45001 illustrate continuing planning, implementation, evaluation and improvement in cooperation with workers. Laws, employee-number conditions, standard editions and certification status change; this textbook alone does not establish current obligations.

food-2-048.activity: Read 10 minutes: organise systems and standards by purpose. Practise 15 minutes: direct quality, environmental, traceability and consultation issues to responsible departments. Check 5 minutes: distinguish a document’s edition from current application conditions.
food-2-048.summary: Distinguish system purposes and connect workplace action to the correct source of updated information.
